readerTitle: Every hire is a bet on the future
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Shopify, 2022년 감원) + 가상 적용 (물류 창고, 소프트웨어 회사) · 비용 수치는 설명용
insight: 채용은 이번 달 비용 한 줄이 아니라 여러 해에 걸친 약속이다. 그래서 업무량 지표와 '정규직 전환 조건'에 묶어 계획한다.
misconception: 일이 늘면 그만큼 바로 사람을 뽑으면 된다. 사람 한 명의 비용은 연봉이다.

sources.text: Tobi Lütke, memo to Shopify employees on layoffs (July 26, 2022), published on the Shopify blog/news site
창고 및 소프트웨어 회사 사례와 비용 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Shopify는 2022년 7월 전체 인력의 약 10%(약 1,000명)를 감원했고, CEO 메모에서 팬데믹 기간 전자상거래 비중이 몇 년 앞당겨진 상태로 유지될 것이라는 베팅이 틀렸으며 그 결정은 자신의 책임이라고 밝혔습니다. 게시 전 원문 메모로 수치와 표현을 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 직접 인용 없이 요약만 적었습니다.
Shopify가 팬데믹 기간 인력을 빠르게 늘렸다는 점은 일반적으로만 서술했습니다. 정확한 연도별 직원 수는 연차보고서로 확인 후 필요하면 추가하세요.
가상 계산: 연봉 $50,000 + 복리후생·급여세 25% $12,500 + 채용·교육 $5,000 = 첫해 $67,500. 67,500 ÷ 50,000 = 1.35배. 25%와 채용·교육비는 설명용 가정이며 국가·업종마다 크게 다릅니다.

cards.title: Every hire is a bet on the future
body: During the pandemic, online shopping jumped. Shopify, which sells software to online stores, grew its team quickly to keep up.
In July 2022, its CEO told staff the company would cut about 10% of its workforce. The reason fits in one line: the hiring had been a bet on the future, and the future turned out differently.

image.label: An office where some desks are suddenly empty
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 사무실 책상들이 줄지어 있고, 일부 책상의 의자만 비어 있음. 벽에는 위로 치솟았다가 꺾이는 선 그래프 포스터. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Orders are up 40%. Do you hire?
body: You run a warehouse that packs orders for online shops. For three months, volume has been 40% above last year. Your team is doing overtime, and your floor manager wants 12 more permanent pickers.

options.text: Hire all 12 as permanent staff now
options.feedback: You fix today's strain fast, but you lock in a year-round cost based on three months of data. If volume falls back, you carry 12 salaries you no longer need.

options.text: Add temps and some overtime now, and hire permanent staff only if volume holds past a set point
options.feedback: You pay a bit more per hour today, but you keep the choice open until the numbers prove the growth is lasting.

options.text: Hire 6 permanent pickers and cover the rest with temps
options.feedback: A sensible hedge, but the number 6 isn't tied to anything. Without a rule for what happens next, it's still a guess.

cards.title: A bet that the surge would last.
body: Shopify's leaders had bet that the pandemic jump in online shopping would stay, as if e-commerce had moved years ahead overnight. They hired for that world.
As shops reopened, growth in online buying slowed. The extra people were now a cost without the extra work to match. In his memo, the CEO said the bet had been his call, and that he had got it wrong.
The lesson isn't that hiring was foolish. It's that **a hiring plan is a forecast** wearing a payroll badge.

cards.title: Planning headcount
body: **Headcount planning** means deciding how many people you need, in which roles, and *when*, based on the work they will do and what they will really cost.
It matters because people are usually a business's biggest cost, and its stickiest. You can cancel an ad campaign next week. Reversing a hire is slow, costly and painful for everyone involved.

image.label: A timeline: decide, recruit, train, fully productive
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 인포그래픽. "Decide to hire" → "Recruit" → "Train" → "Fully productive" 네 단계. 앞 세 단계는 회색, 마지막 단계만 밝은 색. 결정 시점과 실제 생산성 시점 사이의 간격을 화살표로 강조.

cards.title: One hire costs more than one salary.
body: Here the first year costs about **1.35 times** the salary. And a new person usually takes weeks or months to work at full speed, so early output is lower than the cost suggests.

cards.title: Tie people to the work, then to a trigger.
body: A good headcount plan answers three questions:
list: **Driver:** what work grows with this role? Orders per picker per shift, tickets per support agent, deals per sales rep.
**Lead time:** how long to recruit and train? If it's three months, you decide three months early.
**Trigger:** what number must we see before we commit to permanent hires?
cards.callout: Hire for the work you can show, not the growth you hope for.
cards.softwareNote: Software teams often plan hires from revenue targets alone. Linking each role to a driver, like customers per support person, makes it clear which hires the plan truly depends on.

cards.title: Hiring too slowly has a cost too.
body: Waiting for proof isn't free. Overtime often pays a premium, temps may cost more per hour and know less, and tired teams make mistakes and quit.

Some roles also take so long to fill that waiting for a trigger means missing the opportunity. The goal isn't to hire as little as possible. It's to match your commitment to how sure you are, and to know which hires would be hardest to undo.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your software company just raised money. The annual plan calls for 20 new engineers and 15 new salespeople. Your board asks how you will roll out the hiring.

options.text: Hire everyone in the first quarter to move fast
options.feedback: You gain speed, but your burn rate jumps before you know whether new salespeople can actually close deals. If they can't, you've spent runway on a guess.

options.text: Hire in waves, and add each wave of sales hires only after earlier reps hit a revenue target
options.feedback: It's slower at the start, but each wave is backed by evidence, and you can stop before the cost gets ahead of the results.

options.text: Freeze hiring until the company is profitable
options.feedback: You protect cash, but you may lose the growth the money was raised for. Some engineers take months to find and train.

cards.title: Plan people by the work, the full cost and the timing.
body: A hire is a long commitment. Link each role to the work it covers, count its full cost, and decide in advance what evidence turns a temporary fix into a permanent job.
**Try it today:** pick your next planned hire. Write down its full first-year cost, the work number that justifies it, and the level that number must reach first.
